title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response & Evidence Workflows
author: Morgan Li
content:
Summary

Purpose: This document consolidates Redwood Inferenceâ€™s operational security and compliance controls for role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) controls, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence collection workflows, and the process for risk and exceptions. It is intended for platform owners, engineering managers, SRE, security engineers, and compliance reviewers.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood-managed systems and services (hosted API, Dedicated control plane, Private deployment control plane) and to supporting cloud accounts, CI/CD pipelines, logging infrastructure, and evidence repositories.

Owners & Contacts

- Doc owner: Morgan Li (security)
- Primary contacts: Security Oncall (security-oncall@redwood.ai), Platform SRE (sre-platform@redwood.ai)
- Evidence owner for audits: Compliance Manager (compliance@redwood.ai)

1) RBAC & Authentication

Overview and principles
- Principle of least privilege: grant the minimum access required for a role to perform duties.
- Role-based grouping: prefer roles and groups over individual IAM grants.
- Just-in-time elevation: use time-limited admin sessions (e.g., identity provider (IdP) approval or ephemeral keys) for elevated operations.
- Multi-factor authentication (MFA): required for all interactive sign-in and for service accounts with write/admin privileges.

Roles matrix (summary)
- platform-admin: full control over production infra and deployments (restricted, MFA + JIT).
- infra-engineer: manage infrastructure IaC and CI pipelines (no access to customer data stores by default).
- service-operator: deploy and operate runtime services, view runtime metrics/logs.
- support-analyst: read-only access to customer metadata and support tools (no secrets or raw customer files).

Example IAM policy (cloud-native example, illustrative)
- AWS IAM snippet (JSON):
  {
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
      {
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Action": [
          "ec2:DescribeInstances",
          "sts:AssumeRole"
        ],
        "Resource": "*"
      }
    ]
  }

Authentication and service principals
- All CI/CD and service principals must use short-lived credentials (OIDC for GitHub Actions / GCP Workload Identity).
- Long-lived keys are forbidden except for hardware-backed HSM/KMS keys.

RBAC change process
1. Submit an access request (internal access portal) with justification and owner.
2. Approving manager reviews; security approves for sensitive scopes.
3. Access is set with a time-limited expiration (90 days max unless renewed).
4. Periodic access review every 90 days by role owners.

2) Audit Logging

What to log
- Authentication events: successful/failed logins, MFA events, token issuance/refresh.
- Privileged actions: role changes, IAM policy edits, admin console usage, key creation/rotation.
- Administrative API calls: create/delete deployments, model rollback, config changes.
- Data access to classified stores (read/write/delete) and export actions.
- CI/CD pipeline run metadata (who triggered, commits, artifact hashes).

Central logging architecture
- Ingestion: Cloud audit logs (CloudTrail / GCP Audit Logs) -> Fluentd -> Log pipeline -> Datadog & long-term archive in encrypted object storage (s3://redwood-logs-archive).
- Real-time monitoring: Datadog dashboards and correlation rules. Critical alerts route to PagerDuty security-oncall.

Retention and integrity
- Retention SLOs:
  | Classification | Retention | Storage | Responsible |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Auth & Admin logs | 7 years | Encrypted archive (immutable) | security |
  | Operational logs | 2 years | Hot logs in Datadog + archive | sre |
  | CI/CD artifacts & pipeline logs | 3 years | Encrypted archive | eng-platform |
- Tamper evidence: write-once/archive buckets with Object Lock (WORM) enabled for audit-critical logs. Hash manifests are stored in the evidence vault.

Example query (Datadog):
- Failed logins over 24h: query "@event.name:AuthFailure AND @source:identity" | rollup(count)

3) Data Residency & Retention

Residency by environment
- Production PII and customer data: stored and processed in region pinned to customer (e.g., eu-west-1 for EU customers), unless customer permits cross-region processing.
- Non-sensitive telemetry and aggregated metrics: global processing allowed.

Data classification and retention schedule
- PII / Customer Confidential: 7 years by default; deletion after contract termination per DSR/contract.
- Logs containing PII: redact at ingest where possible; if retained, follow the PII retention schedule above.
- Metrics/telemetry (non-PII): 2 years.

Retention enforcement (example automation)
- Retention policies are implemented as lifecycle rules on object stores and via scheduled jobs for database record expiry.
- Example S3 lifecycle JSON rule:
  {
    "Rules": [
      {
        "ID": "pii-retention-rule",
        "Prefix": "customer-data/pii/",
        "Status": "Enabled",
        "Expiration": { "Days": 2555 }
      }
    ]
  }

Data deletion verification
- Deletion jobs produce a signed deletion manifest (hashes of removed objects) persisted to the evidence bucket and registered in the retention audit log.

4) Secure SDLC Requirements

Minimum pre-merge checks
- Mandatory code review by a different approver.
- Static analysis: Snyk/Optic or equivalent; block on high/severe findings.
- Secrets scanning: detect accidental secrets in PRs (git-secrets / TruffleHog).
- Dependency policy: disallow deprecated packages and require approval for transitive dependencies with high CVSS.

CI/CD gating and deployment policy
- All production deployments require a signed CI job using OIDC.
- Canary rollouts with automatic rollback on error thresholds: 5xx rate > 1% or latency P95 increase > 50% in the canary window triggers rollback.
- Post-deploy smoke tests and automated canary verification.

Dependency and build artifact provenance
- Every build records: git commit SHA, builder identity (OIDC subject), artifact checksum, base image digest. These are stored as part of the build metadata and retained for 3 years.

5) Incident Response (Security) Procedures

High-level process
1. Detect: alerting from monitoring, customer report, or third-party notification.
2. Triage: determine scope (affected services, customers, data exposure).
3. Contain: isolate affected systems, rotate keys/credentials if necessary.
4. Remediate: apply fixes, restore from known-good artifacts, patch vulnerabilities.
5. Recover: validate system health and run full QA checks.
6. Review & Lessons Learned: post-incident review and update runbooks.

Forensic preservation checklist
- Preserve snapshots of affected VMs/containers and capture disk images where required.
- Export full audit logs for the timeframe (hash and store in evidence vault).
- Record timeline with actor identities (from IAM logs) and command history (shell history if applicable).

Escalation & SLA thresholds
- Security event classification:
  - Critical (data exfiltration, production compromise): pager to security-oncall, response target: 15 minutes.
  - High (privilege escalation, targeted compromise): pager to security-oncall, response target: 60 minutes.
  - Medium/Low: Slack notification and ticket; triage within 24 hours.

Communication templates
- Incident notification: templated email/portal post with summary, scope, mitigations, and next steps.
- Customer-facing disclosure: coordinate with legal and customer success; include timeline, data impact, and remediation steps.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Evidence types & storage
- Evidence artifacts: IAM change logs, audit log extracts, build provenance, vulnerability scan reports, patch records, policy attestations, exception approvals.
- Storage: encrypted evidence bucket (s3://redwood-evidence) with RBAC-limited access; metadata register stored in the compliance tracker (spreadsheet/issue tracker).

Audit readiness checklist (routine)
1. Quarterly evidence bundle: collect and snapshot required artifacts for common frameworks (SOC2, ISO27001).
2. Evidence owner verifies completeness and signs off in the compliance tracker.
3. Archive signed bundle with team approvals and hash manifest.

Example evidence collection CLI (pseudo):
- export-audit-bundle --start=2026-01-01 --end=2026-03-31 --out=/tmp/audit-bundle-2026-q1.tar.gz

Evidence retention & access
- Evidence for completed audits: retain 7 years. Access requires approval from Compliance Manager.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

Temporary exception lifecycle
1. Submit exception request: include scope, duration, compensating controls, and risk owner.
2. Security evaluates risk; platform/infra owner provides mitigation plan.
3. Approval: Security + Compliance sign-off required for high-risk exceptions.
4. Expiry & Review: automatic expiry (max 90 days) unless renewed with justification.

Risk register entry template (fields)
- id, title, owner, risk_description, impact, likelihood, mitigations, compensating_controls, approved_by, approval_date, expiry_date, status

Example exception JSON (stored in register):
  {
    "id": "EXC-2026-118",
    "title": "Short-term bypass of dependency upgrade",
    "owner": "eng-platform",
    "risk_description": "Temporarily allow dependency X v1.2 due to regression blocking release",
    "impact": "Medium",
    "likelihood": "Low",
    "mitigations": "Runtime WAF rule and additional monitoring",
    "approved_by": "security",
    "approval_date": "2026-11-15",
    "expiry_date": "2027-02-13",
    "status": "active"
  }
